teile.einleitung: A minute is a unit of time and lasts exactly 60 seconds. Sixty minutes make an hour. We use minutes every day to read the clock, catch the bus or brush our teeth for long enough.
wichtigste: A minute has 60 seconds, and an hour has 60 minutes.
The symbol for minute is min.
A quarter of an hour has 15 minutes, three quarters of an hour have 45 minutes.
An hour and a half is 90 minutes.
A day has 1440 minutes.
You should brush your teeth for about 2 to 3 minutes.
Dividing into 60 comes from the ancient Babylonians.

abschnitte.text: The **minute** is a unit of time. It lasts exactly 60 **seconds**, and 60 minutes make an **hour**. So a whole day with 24 hours has 24 times 60, which is 1440 minutes. It is written in short as min, for example 5 min. The word comes from the Latin pars minuta prima, which means “first small part”.

On a clock with hands, the long hand shows the minutes. It takes one hour to go all the way round, and each small mark on the clock face stands for one minute. There are 5 minutes between two numbers. A **quarter of an hour** has 15 minutes, half an hour has 30 minutes. On a digital clock, the minutes come after the colon or, in Switzerland, often after a full stop, such as 10.50.

When you calculate with time, remember that a new hour begins after 59 minutes. For example, it is 10.50, and 20 minutes later it is 11.10, because 10 minutes are missing until the full hour and then another 10 are added. An hour and a half is 60 plus 30, so 90 minutes. A football match lasts two halves of 45 minutes, which is also 90 minutes. You need calculations like these when reading timetables, for example.

The fact that an hour has 60 minutes goes back to the **Babylonians** in ancient Mesopotamia. They used a number system based on the number 60, the **sexagesimal system**. The number 60 can be divided by many numbers: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30. That is why an hour can easily be split into halves, thirds or quarters. However, clocks with minute hands only became common in the 17th century, when clocks became more accurate.

A famous example of the minute is the **Swiss railway clock**, which Hans Hilfiker designed for the SBB in 1944. Its red second hand with the round disc goes round a little faster than one minute. At the top, at the 12, it stops briefly until a signal arrives. Then the minute hand jumps forward one minute, and all the clocks in the country show the new minute at the same time. This way the trains leave on time to the minute.

The word minute is also used when measuring **angles**. A degree is divided into 60 minutes of arc, just like an hour. This is needed, for example, for coordinates on maps and at sea. The minute of time and the minute of arc have the same origin in the Babylonian number system. For angles, you write a small dash, for example 30 degrees and 15 minutes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The 60th part of a minute.
15 minutes, a quarter of an hour.
A number system based on the number 60.
The surface of a clock with the numbers and marks.

gewusst: Because of the leap second, a minute has already had 61 seconds several times.
A child's heart beats about 80 to 100 times in a minute.
The SBB railway clock is so well known that its design has also been used for wristwatches.

teile.einleitung: The money of Switzerland is the Swiss franc, which is divided into 100 centimes (Rappen). There are seven coins and six different banknotes. The coins are minted by Swissmint in Bern, and the banknotes are issued by the Swiss National Bank.
wichtigste: The currency of Switzerland is the Swiss franc, abbreviated CHF.
One franc has 100 centimes (Rappen).
There are coins worth 5, 10 and 20 centimes and ½, 1, 2 and 5 francs.
The five-franc piece is the largest Swiss coin; the most drops of water fit on it.
The banknotes come in 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs.
The coins are minted by Swissmint in Bern; the banknotes are issued by the Swiss National Bank.
The franc has been the common currency of the whole of Switzerland since 1850.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland has seven **coins**: 5, 10 and 20 centimes and ½, 1, 2 and 5 francs. The 5-centime piece is gold-coloured; the other coins are silvery. The centime coins show the head of the goddess of liberty, Libertas. The ½, 1 and 2-franc pieces show Helvetia, a female figure who represents Switzerland. The five-franc piece shows the head of an alpine herdsman and is popularly called the **Fünfliber**.

You can do an exciting experiment with coins: how many drops of water fit on a coin? Using a pipette, you carefully drip water onto it. The water bulges upwards like a dome before it overflows. The reason is **surface tension**: the water particles hold on to each other like a thin skin. The most drops fit on the five-franc piece, because it has the largest surface.

The banknotes come in 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs. The current ninth series was introduced between 2016 and 2019. Each note has a theme that shows the many sides of Switzerland, for example time, light, wind, water, matter and communication. A hand and a globe can be found on all the notes. The 1000-franc note is one of the banknotes with the highest value in the world.

Banknotes have many **security features** so that they are hard to forge. These include a security thread, shiny elements that change colour when you tilt them, and raised printing you can feel. If you hold a note up to the light, you can see a Swiss cross. The coins also have features on the edge. The edge of the Fünfliber bears the inscription “Dominus providebit”, which means “The Lord will provide”.

The coins are made by **Swissmint**, the federal mint in Bern. The banknotes are issued by the **Swiss National Bank** and printed in Zurich. Before the Swiss franc existed in 1850, many cantons had their own money. That made paying complicated, because you constantly had to convert. The 1-centime coin was abolished in 2007 because it was hardly used any more.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hundredth part of a franc.
The everyday name for the five-franc piece.
The force with which water particles hold together at the surface.
The federal mint in Bern, which strikes the Swiss coins.
The state's bank, which issues the money and keeps the franc stable.

gewusst: Swiss coins have looked almost the same for over a hundred years.
The abbreviation CHF comes from “Confoederatio Helvetica” and franc.

teile.einleitung: A bed of nails is a board with a great many sharp nails sticking out of it close together. Amazingly, you can lie down on it without getting hurt. The bed of nails is a well-known example of how pressure depends on the size of the area.
wichtigste: On a bed of nails, the body's weight is spread over a great many points.
Pressure is force divided by area.
The more nails carry the weight, the smaller the force on each single nail.
All the nails must be exactly the same height, or a few nails carry the whole weight.
When standing, the pressure on the soles of the feet is greater than when lying down.
The bed of nails is known as a trick performed by fakirs.
The word fakir comes from Arabic and means “poor”.

abschnitte.titel: What is a bed of nails
abschnitte.text: A bed of nails is a wooden board with hundreds or even thousands of nails whose points face upwards. The nails are only a few centimetres apart and all the same length. Anyone who carefully lies down on it feels many small points but does not get hurt. It is often shown in shows, museums and physics lessons.

abschnitte.titel: Pressure is force divided by area
abschnitte.text: **Pressure** tells you how strongly a force presses on a certain area. It is calculated as force divided by area, and the unit is the **pascal**. If the area is small, the pressure becomes large; if it is large, the pressure becomes small. A single nail has a tiny point and so easily pierces the skin.

If a person with a weight of 600 newtons lies evenly on 600 nails, each nail carries only 1 newton. That is about the weight of a bar of chocolate. If 500 newtons are spread over 1000 points, each with an area of 1 mm², the pressure is **500,000 pascals**. That is not enough to pierce the skin, but a single nail carrying the whole weight would go in deep.

On a board with only a few nails, each nail would have to carry much more weight, which would be dangerous. The height must be right too: if one nail sticks out further, it carries a large part of the load on its own. If you stand on the board instead of lying, the whole weight rests on the small soles of your feet and the pressure becomes greater. That is why you should never try such experiments without guidance from experts.

Lying on beds of nails is often linked with **fakirs**. The word comes from the Arabic word for “poor” and originally meant religious begging monks. In India, some ascetics showed how they could bear pain. Later, the bed of nails became a popular trick in the circus and at fairs.

abschnitte.titel: The same principle in everyday life
abschnitte.text: Stepping barefoot on a small toy brick hurts a lot, because the whole weight presses on a tiny area. **Snowshoes**, on the other hand, spread the weight over a large area so that you do not sink into the snow. Wide tyres on tractors protect the ground for the same reason. Knives and needles work the other way round: their fine edge or point creates enormous pressure.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force acting on a certain area.
The unit of pressure, one newton per square metre.
Originally a poor, religious begging monk; today also a performer who lies on nails.
The force with which the Earth pulls an object downwards.

gewusst: Because the weight is spread over many points, usually only small red dots are left on the skin after getting up.
A bed with only a few nails is more dangerous than one with many nails.
There are mats with many small plastic spikes that people lie on to relax.

teile.einleitung: A multimeter is a measuring device that can measure several electrical quantities. You use it to check voltage, current and resistance. Electricians, hobbyists and physics classes use it every day.
wichtigste: A multimeter measures several electrical quantities, mainly voltage, current and resistance.
The black test lead usually goes into the COM socket.
A straight line next to the symbol stands for direct current, a wavy line for alternating current.
If you do not know how big a value is, you first choose the largest measuring range.
Resistance is only measured with the circuit switched off, because the device itself produces a measuring current.
A minus sign for direct voltage shows that the leads are swapped.
For large currents, you put the red lead into the 10A socket.
In a continuity test, the device beeps if a wire is connected all the way through.

abschnitte.text: The word **multimeter** means something like multiple meter. In the past, you needed a separate device each for voltage, current and resistance. Today, all the functions are in one handy box with a rotary switch. Most devices show the value as a number on a display; older ones have a pointer.

The black lead goes into the **COM** socket, which stands for common. Depending on the measurement, the red lead goes into the socket for volts and ohms or for amperes. There is a separate 10A socket for large currents. On the rotary switch, V stands for voltage, A for current and the omega sign for resistance, with a straight line for direct current and a wavy line for alternating current.

**Voltage** is measured in parallel, so you hold the tips to two points, for example to the terminals of a battery. **Current** is measured in series: the current must flow through the device. Resistance is only measured without current, because the multimeter sends a small measuring current through itself. If you do not know the value, you start in the largest range and then switch down.

In a **continuity test**, the device beeps if there is a connection between two points. This lets you quickly find a broken cable or a blown fuse. A minus sign in front of the value shows that the leads are swapped, but with direct voltage this does no harm. Some devices also measure temperature or test diodes.

The units of the measured quantities are named after scientists. The volt recalls the Italian Alessandro Volta, who built the first battery. The ampere honours the Frenchman André-Marie Ampère, and the ohm the German Georg Simon **Ohm**. A fresh AA battery shows about 1.5 volts, a flat one clearly less.

A socket in Switzerland carries 230 volts of alternating voltage, which is life-threatening. Such measurements should only be made by experts with suitable devices. At school, you measure with batteries and small power supplies. Before every measurement, you check that the leads and tips are undamaged.

begriffe.erklaerung: The electrical pressure that drives the current, measured in volts.
How much electric charge flows per second, measured in amperes.
How strongly a component slows down the current, measured in ohms.
The range of values the device can measure at one setting.
A test to see whether a cable or wire is connected all the way through.

gewusst: For measuring voltage, a good multimeter has a very high internal resistance so that it hardly changes the circuit.
Devices set to measure current, on the other hand, have almost no resistance, which is why a wrong setting can destroy the built-in fuse.

teile.einleitung: Magnetic declination is the angle between the direction a compass needle points and the direction to the geographic North Pole. It exists because the magnetic North Pole is not in the same place as the geographic one. Another name for it is magnetic variation.
wichtigste: Magnetic declination is the angle between magnetic north and geographic north.
Another technical term for it is variation.
It changes over the years, because the Earth's magnetic poles move.
In Switzerland it is only a few degrees today.
Lines of equal declination on a map are called isogonic lines.
Sailors and pilots have to take it into account carefully when navigating.
Close to a magnetic pole, the declination can become very large.

abschnitte.text: A **compass needle** is a small magnet and lines itself up with the Earth's magnetic field. So it points to the magnetic North Pole, not exactly to the geographic North Pole around which the Earth turns. The angle between these two directions is called **magnetic declination** or variation. If the needle points east of geographic north, it is called easterly declination, otherwise westerly.

The Earth's magnetic field is created by currents of liquid iron deep inside the Earth. These currents change slowly, so the magnetic North Pole moves. For a long time it was in northern Canada, and for decades it has been moving towards Siberia. That is why the declination is different in every place and changes over time.

In Switzerland today, the compass needle points only a few degrees east of geographic north. For a hike with map and compass, this error is usually small. On accurate national maps, the declination is given at the edge of the map. About a hundred years ago, it was still westerly in Switzerland and clearly larger.

Lines connecting places with the same declination are called **isogonic lines**. The line on which the declination is zero is called the agonic line. Worldwide maps of declination are recalculated regularly because the magnetic field changes. Navigation devices and mobile phones use such models to work out true north from the compass direction.

Sailors and pilots must know the declination precisely, or they would drift far off course on long journeys. In addition, iron parts and electrical devices in the ship or aircraft deflect the needle. This deflection is called **deviation**. Both errors are added together when the course is calculated.

The closer you get to a magnetic pole, the larger the declination can become. In the Arctic, a compass needle can even point almost south or west. Right at the magnetic pole, the needle points steeply down into the ground. There, an ordinary compass is hardly usable for navigation.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another technical word for magnetic declination.
A line on a map connecting places with the same declination.
Deflection of the compass needle by iron or devices in the vehicle.
The place in the north that compass needles point to.

gewusst: At times the magnetic North Pole has moved several dozen kilometres a year.
Centuries ago, sailors already noticed that the compass does not point exactly north.
Runway numbers at airports are based on the magnetic direction and therefore sometimes have to be changed.

teile.einleitung: Instantaneous speed is the speed an object has at one particular moment. This is exactly the number that the speedometer in a car shows. It is often different from the average speed that you calculate for a whole journey.
wichtigste: Instantaneous speed is the speed at a particular moment.
A car's speedometer shows the instantaneous speed.
You measure it by dividing a very short distance by a very short time.
On a distance-time graph, it is the gradient of the curve at one point.
In uniform motion, it is always equal to the average speed.
A ball thrown upwards has an instantaneous speed of zero at its highest point.
A pendulum is fastest at its lowest point.

abschnitte.text: If a car travels 60 kilometres in 1 hour, its **average speed** is 60 km/h. But on the way it was sometimes faster, sometimes slower, and it stood still at traffic lights. The speed at a single moment is called the **instantaneous speed**. The speedometer shows it all the time.

You measure the distance an object travels in a very short time and divide it by that time. The shorter the time span, the more precisely you get the speed at that moment. An example: a car covers a 4-metre measuring section in 0.2 seconds, which is 20 m/s or 72 km/h. Some speed checks work this way too, with **light barriers** or sensors in the road.

On a distance-time graph, you record how far an object has travelled at each point in time. If the curve is steep, the object is fast; if it is flat, it is slow. You can see the instantaneous speed from the **gradient** of the curve at a particular point. In maths this is called the derivative, which Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed in the 17th century.

Without air resistance, a falling stone becomes about 9.8 m/s faster every second. After 3 seconds, its instantaneous speed is 29.4 m/s, which is over 100 km/h. If you throw a ball straight up, it gets slower and slower. At its highest point, its instantaneous speed is exactly **zero** for a moment, and then it falls back down.

On a pendulum or a swing, the speed changes all the time. At the turning points right at the edges, it is briefly zero. At the lowest point, the instantaneous speed is greatest, because there most of the potential energy has been turned into kinetic energy. You can feel this on any swing as a brief tingle in your tummy.

On the road, it is always the instantaneous speed that counts, for example at a **speed camera**. Anyone caught doing 70 km/h in town cannot argue that they were only driving at 50 km/h on average. When skiing, cycling or in space travel, the speed at the moment is also important. Sports watches and mobile phones work it out, for example, with the help of GPS.

begriffe.erklaerung: Total distance divided by total time.
A display in a vehicle that shows the current speed.
Movement at an unchanging speed in the same direction.
How steeply a curve on a graph rises at one point.

gewusst: When a ball briefly stops at its highest point, gravity is still acting on it.
A speedometer usually shows a little more than you are actually doing, because it must never show too little.
A cheetah can run at over 90 km/h for a short moment, but can only keep up this speed for a few seconds.

teile.einleitung: Food energy is the energy contained in what we eat and drink. Our body needs it to grow, move and think, and even while sleeping to breathe and keep warm. Food packaging shows how much energy a product contains, usually in kilocalories and kilojoules.
wichtigste: The body needs energy for everything it does, even during sleep.
On packaging, energy is given in kilocalories and kilojoules.
Carbohydrates, fats and proteins provide energy.
Fat contains more than twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates.
Nuts are particularly rich in energy.
Pure water contains no energy at all.
People who move a lot need more energy from their food.

abschnitte.text: Plants store the energy of sunlight in sugar and starch. When we eat plants or animals, our body takes in this stored energy. In the cells, it is released slowly with the help of oxygen, a bit like a very gentle burning. This is how muscles, brain and heart get the energy they need.

Energy is provided by three groups of nutrients. **Carbohydrates** are found in bread, pasta, rice and potatoes and give the body energy for everyday life. **Fats** in butter, oil and nuts provide about 9 kilocalories per gram, more than twice as much as carbohydrates or proteins with about 4 kilocalories. Water, vitamins and minerals are important but provide no energy.

On food packaging, the **nutrition table** shows how much energy there is in 100 grams. It is given in kilocalories, abbreviated kcal, and in kilojoules, abbreviated kJ. One kilocalorie is about 4.2 kilojoules. 100 grams of nuts often have over 600 kilocalories, 100 grams of apples only about 50.

abschnitte.titel: What the body needs energy for
abschnitte.text: Even when we sleep, the body needs energy for breathing, heartbeat and **body heat**; this is called the basal metabolic rate. On top of that comes energy for movement, sport and thinking, because the brain uses a lot of energy. Children also need extra energy to grow. A child playing football needs more energy than one sitting still.

Sweets give energy quickly but harm your teeth in large amounts and do not keep you full for long. Wholemeal bread, potatoes, vegetables and pulses release their energy more slowly and keep you full for longer. If you go a long time without eating, you feel tired and weak and find it hard to concentrate. The Swiss **food pyramid** shows how to eat a varied and balanced diet.

If you eat more energy than you use over a long time, the body stores it as fat. If you eat too little, you lack the strength to grow and learn. The best thing is a balance between eating and exercise. How much energy you need depends on your age, size and how much you move.

begriffe.erklaerung: A unit for the energy in food, abbreviated kcal.
The physical unit of energy, abbreviated kJ.
The energy the body needs when completely at rest.
Nutrients such as sugar and starch that provide energy quickly.
The table on the packet showing energy and nutrients.

gewusst: The brain makes up only about 2 per cent of body weight but uses around 20 per cent of the energy at rest.
You can measure the energy content of a food by burning it completely in a calorimeter and measuring the heat produced.
The body also uses extra energy when you are cold, because the shivering of the muscles produces heat.

teile.einleitung: Reverberation time tells you how long a sound keeps ringing in a room after the source of the sound has stopped. In an empty church, a clap echoes for a long time; in a room with carpet and curtains, hardly at all. The right reverberation time is very important for concert halls, classrooms and theatres.
wichtigste: Reverberation time is the time it takes for the sound level to fall by 60 decibels after the sound stops.
Wallace Clement Sabine founded scientific room acoustics around 1900.
According to Sabine's formula, T = 0.161 · V / A.
If you double the absorption area, the reverberation time is halved.
Large concert halls for symphonies have a reverberation time of about 2 seconds.
In classrooms, too long a reverberation time makes speech harder to understand.
Soft materials such as curtains, carpets and upholstery absorb sound.

abschnitte.text: Sound spreads out in a room and is **reflected** again and again by the walls, ceiling and floor. That is why you still hear a sound for a while even when the source is already silent. With each reflection, part of the sound is absorbed, until the sound disappears. The **reverberation time** measures how long it takes for the level to fall by 60 decibels, that is to a millionth of the sound intensity.

The American physicist **Wallace Clement Sabine** lived from 1868 to 1919 and taught at Harvard University. He was asked to improve a lecture hall in which the speakers could hardly be understood. Using seat cushions, a stopwatch and his own hearing, he studied how materials change the reverberation. From this, around 1900, he developed his formula and then advised on the building of Symphony Hall in Boston.

The formula is T = 0.161 · V / A, where V is the volume of the room in cubic metres and A is the **equivalent absorption area** in square metres. A room of 1000 m³ with 200 m² of absorption area has a reverberation time of about 0.8 seconds. The absorption area of a wall is its area times its absorption coefficient, so for 50 m² and 0.3 it is 15 m². If a room of 600 m³ is to have a reverberation time of 1.2 seconds, it needs about 80 m² of absorption area.

For symphonic music in large concert halls, people want about **2 seconds** of reverberation so that the music sounds full and warm. Large churches often echo much longer, which is lovely for organ music but difficult for speech. The concert hall in the KKL in Lucerne is famous worldwide for its very good acoustics. There, the acoustics can even be adapted to the music with movable flaps and chambers.

In classrooms, a short reverberation time of well under a second is important. If it is too long, the words blur together and **speech intelligibility** falls. Children then have to make more effort, and the room becomes louder overall. That is why acoustic ceilings, wall panels made of porous material or pinboards are fitted.

Hard, smooth surfaces such as concrete, glass and tiles reflect sound almost completely. Soft and porous materials such as carpets, curtains, upholstered furniture or acoustic foam **absorb** it. People absorb sound too, which is why a full hall sounds different from an empty one. You can try this at home by clapping your hands in an empty room and in a furnished room.

begriffe.erklaerung: The time in which a sound in a room becomes 60 decibels quieter.
The soaking up of sound by a material.
The unit for loudness, or sound level.
The study of how rooms sound.
The bouncing back of sound from a surface.

gewusst: A room with no reverberation, a so-called anechoic chamber, feels eerily silent to many people.
Because people absorb sound, concert seats are often upholstered so that the hall sounds similar whether it is empty or full.
The unit “sabin” for absorption area is named after Wallace Clement Sabine.

teile.einleitung: A marble run is a track on which small balls, the marbles, roll down through channels, bends and tunnels. You can buy one or simply build one yourself out of cardboard. While doing so, you learn a lot in a playful way about gravity, speed and friction.
wichtigste: On a marble run, marbles roll along: small balls made of glass, wood or clay.
For a marble to roll by itself, the track must slope downwards.
You can easily build your own marble run from cardboard tubes.
On bends, the track needs high edges, or fast marbles fly out.
If a marble has to roll uphill, it slows down.
On a flat carpet, the marble slows down and comes to a stop.
Lots of zigzag bends make the ride long.

abschnitte.text: A **marble run**, also called a ball track, is made of channels, tubes or building blocks with grooves. You put a **marble** in at the top, and it comes out again at the bottom. On the way, it rolls through bends, tunnels, funnels and sometimes over switches. In Switzerland, marbles are also called Chlicker.

**Gravity** always pulls the marble downwards. If the track slopes, the ball rolls downhill and gets faster. The steeper the slope, the faster it gets. If it has to go uphill for a bit, it slows down and only makes it if it has enough momentum.

A fast marble wants to keep going straight on at a bend. High edges or banked bends keep it on the track, like on a bobsleigh run. On a flat carpet, **friction** slows the ball down until it stops. On smooth wood or plastic, it rolls much further.

You can build your own track out of **cardboard tubes** from kitchen roll, sticky tape and a wall. You cut the tubes open lengthways and stick them below each other at a slant and in a zigzag. The more bends, the longer the marble is on its way. With a stopwatch, you can measure which design gives the longest ride.

The Swiss company **Cuboro** makes well-known marble runs out of wooden cubes. Grooves and tunnels are milled into the cubes, which can be put together in new ways again and again. There are also plastic systems and huge marble runs in museums and playgrounds. While building, you practise planning, trying things out and working carefully.

Around 400 years ago, the scientist **Galileo Galilei** rolled balls down sloping channels. In this way he studied how objects get faster and faster as they fall. On a marble run, you can see how height is turned into movement. If, for example, 3 red and 4 blue marbles roll, that makes 7 altogether, and you can hold races between them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small ball made of glass, clay, wood or stone for playing with.
The force with which the Earth pulls everything downwards.
A force that slows down movement when two things rub against each other.
How steeply a track is tilted downwards.

gewusst: Marbles are among the oldest toys in the world; children in ancient Egypt and ancient Rome already played with them.
On a track, a marble never quite rolls back up to the same height it started from, because friction always takes away some energy.

teile.einleitung: A mobile is a hanging, moving work of art made of rods, threads and figures that float in balance. Even a light draught makes it turn and sway. The American artist Alexander Calder made this art form famous.
wichtigste: A mobile is a hanging, moving work of art.
The name comes from “mobile”, which means able to move.
Alexander Calder made the mobile famous in the 1930s.
A draught sets a mobile moving without a motor.
For a mobile to hang level, the weights must balance according to the law of the lever.
If a rod hangs at a slant, you move the hanging thread closer to the heavier figure.
A mobile often hangs above a baby's cot.

abschnitte.text: A mobile is made of several horizontal rods with figures or more rods hanging from their ends. Everything hangs on threads from the ceiling. The parts turn freely and do not touch each other. Because the picture keeps changing, the mobile is also called **kinetic art**, which means art of movement.

The American artist **Alexander Calder** lived from 1898 to 1976. He had first studied mechanical engineering and so understood balance and technology. In the early 1930s, he built his first hanging works of art from wire and painted sheet metal in Paris. The artist Marcel Duchamp gave them the name “mobile”.

Each rod of a mobile is a **lever** that hangs from its thread as if from a pivot. It hangs level when weight times distance is the same on both sides. So two fish of equal weight at the same distance from the middle keep the rod level. If one figure is heavier, it has to hang closer to the hanging point, which is why you move the thread towards the heavy side.

A mobile does not need a motor. A light **draught** from an open window or warm rising air is enough. Because the parts are so finely balanced, a tiny force is enough to make them turn. The movements are slow and calm, which is why mobiles often have a soothing effect.

Many parents hang a mobile above a baby's cot. Babies enjoy following the shapes and colours with their eyes. Mobiles also hang as decorations in classrooms, shops and museums. Large mobiles by Calder hang, for example, in museums and entrance halls in the USA and in Europe.

You can make a simple mobile from **twigs**, threads and paper figures. It is best to start at the bottom with the smallest rod and balance it. Then you hang this part from a larger rod and balance it again. This way, a floating work of art grows level by level.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rod that moves around a pivot and can balance forces.
A state in which all forces cancel each other out and nothing tips over.
Works of art that move.
The point a lever turns around; in a mobile, the hanging thread.

gewusst: As a young man, Calder also built a small circus out of wire, with which he gave performances.
Calder's counterparts to mobiles, which stand firmly on the ground, are called stabiles.
Some of Calder's mobiles are several metres in size and weigh hundreds of kilograms.

teile.einleitung: Muscle power is the force that people and animals produce with their muscles. We use it to walk, jump, lift and breathe. Long before there were engines, the muscle power of people and animals was the most important driving force in the world.
wichtigste: We move our bodies with our muscles.
Humans have more than 600 muscles.
Most muscles are attached to the bones by tendons.
Muscles can only pull, not push, which is why they work in pairs.
The heart is a muscle that works without a break for a whole lifetime.
The largest human muscle is the gluteus maximus, the big buttock muscle.
A bicycle without a motor is driven by muscle power alone.

abschnitte.text: A muscle is made up of many long **muscle fibres** that can contract. As they do, the muscle becomes shorter and thicker and pulls on a bone. The commands for this come from the brain through the nerves. The muscle gets the energy for this from food and from the oxygen that the blood brings.

Most muscles are attached to the bones by **tendons**. Because muscles can only pull, there is always an opposing muscle. The **biceps** on the upper arm bends the arm, and the triceps on the back straightens it again. Bones and joints act like levers, very much as in physics.

We move skeletal muscles on purpose, for example when walking or throwing. Smooth muscles work by themselves, for example in the stomach and intestines. A special kind is the **heart muscle**, which pumps around the clock without getting tired. In children at rest, it beats about 80 to 100 times a minute.

Humans have more than 600 muscles; in adults they make up about a third to almost half of body weight. The largest is the **gluteus maximus**, the big buttock muscle, which helps us stand up and climb stairs. The smallest muscle is in the ear and is only a few millimetres long. For their size, the chewing muscles are among the strongest muscles.

A bicycle, a rowing boat or a scooter without a motor runs on muscle power alone. In the past, horses and oxen pulled ploughs and carts, and people carried heavy loads on their backs. In Switzerland, muleteers carried goods with mules over Alpine passes such as the Gotthard. Muscle power is clean and quiet and produces no exhaust fumes.

If you do sport regularly, you make your muscles stronger and give them more stamina. After an unusual amount of exercise, you often feel **sore muscles** the next day. This is caused by tiny injuries in the muscle fibres, which the body repairs within a few days. Enough sleep, protein in your food and warming up before sport help the muscles.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long, thin cell that can contract.
A tough band that connects a muscle to a bone.
A muscle that reverses the movement of another muscle.
Pain in the muscles after unusual effort.

gewusst: Breathing also happens with muscle power, because the diaphragm contracts and lets air flow into the lungs.
Dozens of muscles are also at work at the same time when you speak.
The tongue is made almost entirely of muscles.

teile.einleitung: The mixing temperature is the temperature reached when you bring a warm and a cold substance together. If you mix hot and cold water, the result lies somewhere in between. With a simple rule, you can work out exactly where.
wichtigste: The basis is that the heat given off equals the heat taken in.
Equal masses of water at 20 and 60 degrees together give 40 degrees.
The rule for calculating it is named after the physicist Georg Wilhelm Richmann.
The mixing temperature depends on mass, temperature and specific heat capacity.
Water has a very large heat capacity and therefore strongly affects the mixture.
If ice melts in the mixture, extra heat of fusion is needed.
Calculations usually ignore heat lost to the surroundings.

abschnitte.text: When two objects at different temperatures come together, **heat** flows from the warm one to the cold one. This continues until both are equally warm. This shared final temperature is called the **mixing temperature**. It always lies between the two starting temperatures.

The physicist **Georg Wilhelm Richmann** lived in Saint Petersburg in the 18th century. He realised that the heat given off by the warm substance is exactly as large as the heat taken in by the cold one. This leads to **Richmann's mixing rule**. For each substance you multiply mass, heat capacity and temperature, and divide the sum by the sum of mass times heat capacity.

With equal amounts of water, the mixture is exactly in the middle: 20 and 60 degrees give 40 degrees. If you mix 2 kilograms at 10 degrees with 1 kilogram at 70 degrees, you get 30 degrees. 30 litres at 50 degrees and 10 litres at 10 degrees give 40 degrees. The more there is of one kind, the closer the mixture is to its temperature.

Not every substance stores the same amount of heat. This is described by the **specific heat capacity**: for water around 4180 joules per kilogram and degree, for iron only around 450. If you drop 0.1 kilograms of iron at 200 degrees into 0.3 kilograms of water at 20 degrees, the water only rises to about 26 degrees. Even with 1 kilogram of hot water and 1 kilogram of cold copper, the mixture is close to the water temperature.

If you put ice into warm water, the ice first has to melt. This needs the **heat of fusion**, 334 kilojoules per kilogram for ice, without the temperature rising. That is why ice cubes cool a drink so well. 0.1 kilograms of ice in 0.5 kilograms of water at 40 degrees end up at only about 20 degrees.

If you want a bath at 37 degrees and have 50 litres of water at 15 degrees, you need around 48 litres of water at 60 degrees. The rule also helps with tea and cold milk or when cooling a baby's bottle. In reality, some heat is always lost to the air and the container. In the laboratory, it is therefore measured in a well-insulated container, the **calorimeter**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy that flows from a warmer object to a colder one.
How much energy is needed to warm 1 kilogram of a substance by 1 degree.
Energy needed to melt a solid substance.
A well-insulated container in which amounts of heat are measured.

gewusst: Because water can store so much heat, large lakes such as Lake Geneva bring milder winters to their shores.
Georg Wilhelm Richmann was killed in 1753 during an experiment with lightning.

teile.einleitung: Moonlight is the light that reaches us from the Moon at night. But the Moon does not shine by itself; it only reflects sunlight like a big grey mirror. At full moon it is so bright that you can even cast a faint shadow outdoors.
wichtigste: The Moon does not shine by itself; it reflects sunlight.
Moonlight is brightest at full moon.
At new moon, you cannot see the Moon in the sky at all.
Moonlight is much weaker than sunlight.
Light from the Moon takes about one second to reach the Earth.
You cannot get sunburnt in moonlight, because it is too weak.
From the Earth we always see the same side of the Moon.

abschnitte.text: The Moon is a lump of rock with no light of its own. What we see as **moonlight** is sunlight reflected from its surface. The rock is rather dark grey and reflects only a small part of the light, roughly as much as old asphalt. Even so, the Moon looks brilliantly bright against the dark night sky. The light takes only about **one second** to cover the roughly 384,000 kilometres to the Earth.

Moonlight is brightest at **full moon**, when the whole side facing us is lit. At **new moon** we see the unlit side and the Moon is practically invisible. But even the full moon is several hundred thousand times fainter than the Sun. On a clear full-moon night, the light is still enough to cast a faint shadow and to make out your surroundings on a path.

In weak moonlight, our eyes mainly use the **rods**, which tell light from dark but hardly see colours. That is why a moonlit landscape looks almost black and white or slightly bluish. You cannot get sunburnt in moonlight, because it contains far too little ultraviolet radiation. If you go walking at night, it is best to let your eyes get used to the dark without a torch.

The Moon turns once on its own axis in exactly the same time that it takes to orbit the Earth. That is why it always shows us the same side, which is called **tidal locking**. People first saw the far side of the Moon in 1959, in photos from a Soviet space probe. On the near side you can see dark patches with the naked eye, the so-called **maria**, which were once thought to be seas.

Many animals are guided by moonlight, for example nocturnal birds and insects that use it to find their way. In the past, the full moon was important for people because they could travel or work on bright nights. On some clear nights, a **moonbow** even appears, which looks almost white to our eyes. Because of all the artificial lighting in towns, people notice moonlight less today than in the countryside or in the mountains.

begriffe.erklaerung: The phase of the Moon in which the whole visible side of the Moon is lit.
The phase of the Moon in which you cannot see the Moon.
The Moon turns in such a way that it always shows the Earth the same side.
Dark, flat plains on the Moon made of solidified lava.

gewusst: The Moon is actually quite dark; its rock reflects only about an eighth of the sunlight.
When we look at the Moon, we see it as it was just over a second ago.
When there is a thin crescent moon, you can sometimes see the dark part glowing faintly, because light from the Earth falls on it.

teile.einleitung: Fog is a cloud that lies right on the ground. It is made of countless tiny droplets of water that float in the air and make it hard to see. In the Swiss Plateau, fog is so common in autumn and winter that people often talk about a “sea of fog”.
wichtigste: Fog is made of tiny water droplets floating in the air.
It is called fog when visibility falls below one kilometre.
Very light fog with better visibility is called mist.
Fog often forms in the morning over lakes and rivers.
When the Sun warms it up, fog often clears.
In fog, drivers should drive more slowly and leave a bigger gap.
Ships warn each other in thick fog with a foghorn.

abschnitte.text: Air always contains invisible **water vapour**. When the air cools down, it can hold less water vapour, and this condenses into tiny droplets. If these droplets float close to the ground, fog forms. Meteorologists call it fog when visibility falls below one kilometre, otherwise **mist**.

On clear, still nights, the ground cools down a lot, and so does the air above it. This creates **radiation fog**, especially in valleys and hollows. The air over lakes and rivers is damp, which is why fog often forms there in the morning. Fog also forms when warm, damp air flows over cold ground or cold water, for example on sea coasts.

abschnitte.titel: Sea of fog over the Swiss Plateau
abschnitte.text: In autumn and winter, a blanket of fog often lies over the Swiss Plateau for days. Cold air collects between the Jura and the Alps, with warmer air lying above it like a lid; this is called an **inversion**. If the fog does not lie on the ground but a few hundred metres higher up, it is called **high fog**. Anyone who climbs the Uetliberg, Pilatus or the Napf then often sees a beautiful sea of fog in the sunshine.

Fog is dangerous because you only see obstacles and other vehicles late. Drivers should therefore drive more slowly, switch on their lights and increase the **gap** to the car in front. Cars have special fog lights that may only be used in thick fog. At airports, taking off and landing in very thick fog is sometimes difficult, but modern instruments help the pilots.

Ships warn each other in thick fog with a loud **foghorn**. In the past, there were foghorns and bells at lighthouses on dangerous coasts. Today, radar and satellite navigation also help to avoid collisions. On Swiss lakes, passenger boats travel slowly in fog and give sound signals.

On foggy mornings, spider webs suddenly become easy to see, because many tiny water drops cling to the threads. When the Sun warms up the fog, the droplets evaporate and it clears. In fog, sounds seem muffled and the landscape looks mysterious. In some dry parts of the world, people even collect drinking water from fog with nets.

begriffe.erklaerung: When water vapour cools down and turns into liquid droplets.
Light fog in which you can still see more than a kilometre.
Fog that lies like a grey blanket above the ground.
A weather situation in which cold air lies below and warmer air above it.

gewusst: Fog and clouds are made of exactly the same thing; fog is just on the ground.
In the Atacama Desert in Chile and on other dry coasts, nets catch fog droplets as water.
When you walk in fog, your clothes can get wet even though it is not raining at all.

teile.einleitung: The Moon is the Earth's only natural companion and our nearest neighbour in space. It is much smaller than the Earth, and its gravity is only about one sixth as strong. In 1969, with Apollo 11, people walked on its surface for the first time.
wichtigste: On average, the Moon is about 384,000 kilometres from the Earth.
It is about a quarter as wide as the Earth.
Its gravity is only about one sixth of the gravity on Earth.
It takes about four weeks to go once around the Earth.
It has almost no air, because its gravity is too weak.
The Moon's pull causes the tides on Earth.
In 1969, with Apollo 11, the first people landed on the Moon.

abschnitte.text: The Moon has a diameter of about 3474 kilometres, making it about **a quarter as wide** as the Earth. On average it is around **384,000 kilometres** away. Light takes only just over a second to travel this distance. The Moon orbits the Earth in about four weeks and always shows us the same side.

Because the Moon is much smaller and lighter than the Earth, its **gravity** is only about one sixth as strong. A bathroom scale that shows 30 kg on Earth would show only about 5 kg on the Moon. A stone falls more slowly there, and astronauts could make long jumps. The weak gravity can hardly hold on to any air either, which is why the Moon has almost no **atmosphere**.

The large dark areas are called **lunar seas**, even though there is no water there. They are made of solidified lava from the Moon's early days. The bright areas are highlands full of **craters**, which were formed by rocks crashing into them. During the day it gets hotter than 100 °C on the Moon, and at night far colder than 100 °C below zero. Because there is neither wind nor rain, footprints stay for a very long time.

The Moon's pull tugs at the Earth's oceans and creates the **tides**. Depending on how the Sun lights up the Moon, we see it as a full moon, half moon or new moon. These **phases of the Moon** repeat about every 29.5 days. Scientists think that the Moon formed about 4.5 billion years ago after a huge collision between another body and the young Earth.

On 20 July 1969, the **Apollo 11** mission landed in the Sea of Tranquillity. **Neil Armstrong** was the first person to step onto the Moon, followed shortly afterwards by Buzz Aldrin. By 1972, a total of twelve astronauts had been on the Moon. Together they brought several hundred kilograms of moon rock back to Earth.

As the first scientific experiment, Buzz Aldrin set up a **solar wind sail** from the University of Bern. It was a kind of aluminium foil that caught particles from the solar wind. The experiment was led by the Bern physicist **Johannes Geiss**. The Bern sail was also taken along on later Apollo flights.

begriffe.erklaerung: The changing shapes in which we see the lit part of the Moon.
A round hollow formed by an impact.
A large dark plain of solidified lava on the Moon.
The regular rising and falling of the sea level.

gewusst: The Moon moves about 3.8 centimetres further away from the Earth every year.
The far side of the Moon was not photographed until 1959, by a Soviet space probe.
On the Moon, the sky is black even during the day, because there is no air to scatter the light.

teile.einleitung: Minergie is a Swiss building standard for buildings that use very little energy and are still comfortable to live and work in. It has existed since 1998. A house with a Minergie certificate is well insulated, has automatic ventilation and uses renewable energy wherever possible.
wichtigste: Minergie is a Swiss label for energy-efficient buildings.
The standard has existed since 1998.
The Minergie association is supported by the federal government, the cantons and businesses.
Very good thermal insulation and comfort ventilation are important.
As well as low energy use, high living comfort is a stated goal.
Minergie-P has especially strict requirements, similar to a passive house.
The ECO addition also pays attention to health and building ecology.

abschnitte.text: Minergie is a voluntary **label**, a quality mark for buildings. A house only gets it if it follows certain rules on energy use and comfort. This applies to new houses and also to renovated old buildings. Schools, offices and hospitals can also be Minergie-certified.

The most important thing is a well-insulated **building envelope**: the walls, roof, floor and windows. Thick layers of insulation and triple-glazed windows keep the warmth inside in winter and the heat outside in summer. This means much less energy is needed for heating. You can think of it as a thick winter coat for the house.

**Comfort ventilation** is typical of Minergie buildings. It constantly brings fresh air into the house and takes stale air out, without anyone having to open the windows. A heat exchanger takes the warmth from the outgoing air and passes it to the cold fresh air. You can still open the windows at any time.

The basic standard is simply called Minergie. **Minergie-P** requires an even better building envelope and is comparable to a passive house. With Minergie-A, the building produces much of its own energy over the year, usually with solar panels on the roof. The **ECO** addition can be combined with any of the standards and requires healthy, environmentally friendly building materials and plenty of daylight.

In the 1990s, experts in Switzerland developed the idea of a simple standard for economical houses. The Minergie association was founded in 1998. Today it is supported jointly by the federal government, the cantons and businesses. There are now tens of thousands of Minergie buildings in Switzerland.

In Switzerland, buildings use a large share of all energy, mainly for heating and hot water. Using less energy protects the climate and saves on heating costs. Many Minergie houses are heated with heat pumps instead of oil or gas. Some cantons support Minergie buildings with grants.

begriffe.erklaerung: Materials that stop heat escaping through walls and the roof.
A system that automatically brings fresh air into the house and takes stale air out.
A device that passes heat from warm outgoing air to cold fresh air.
A house that is so well insulated that it hardly needs any heating.
A quality mark that confirms certain properties.

gewusst: In a Minergie house, the people, lamps and appliances noticeably help to heat it too.
The filters of a comfort ventilation system also keep out many pollen grains, which helps people with hay fever.
Even old houses can get a Minergie certificate after a good renovation.

teile.einleitung: The phases of the Moon are the different shapes in which we see the Moon in the sky: from a thin crescent to a half moon to a full moon. The Moon does not really change its shape. Depending on the positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon, we simply see a different part of its lit side.
wichtigste: The Moon is always half lit by the Sun.
Depending on the position, we see a larger or smaller part of this lit half.
It takes about 29.5 days from one new moon to the next.
The main phases are called new moon, first quarter, full moon and last quarter.
If the crescent is lit on the right and looks like a bracket “)”, the Moon is waxing.
There are 12 or 13 full moons in a year.
You can often see the Moon during the day too.

abschnitte.titel: How do the phases of the Moon happen?
abschnitte.text: The Sun always lights up exactly one half of the Moon. As the Moon orbits the Earth, we look at it from changing directions. Sometimes we see a lot of the bright side, sometimes a little, sometimes none. This creates the **phases of the Moon**. People often think that the Earth's shadow covers the Moon, but that is not true; that only happens during a lunar eclipse.

About **29.5 days** pass from one new moon to the next. At new moon, the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun and is invisible. After that, a thin **crescent** appears in the evening, growing day by day until, after about a week, you can see the waxing **half moon**. Around two weeks after new moon it is **full moon**; after that the Moon wanes again to the waning half moon and the next new moon.

In the northern hemisphere, which includes Switzerland, the rule is: if the right side is bright and the crescent looks like a bracket “)”, the Moon is waxing. If the left side is bright, like “(”, it is waning. An old German memory aid says that if you can add one stroke to make a handwritten **a**, the Moon is waning (abnehmen means to wane). In the southern hemisphere, for example in Australia, it is exactly the other way round.

You can often see the Moon during the **day** too, for example the waxing half moon in the afternoon or the waning one in the morning. It looks pale then, because the bright sky outshines it. Only around new moon can you not see it at all, because it is almost in the same direction as the Sun. The full moon, on the other hand, rises at about sunset and sets at about sunrise.

Because the Moon returns so regularly, many peoples based their **calendars** on it. Our word “month” comes from the word moon. The Islamic calendar is still a pure lunar calendar today, and the date of Easter depends on the first full moon in spring. As a lunar month is shorter than most calendar months, there are sometimes two full moons in one month; the second is often called a **blue moon**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The shape in which we see the lit part of the Moon.
The thin, curved shape of the Moon shortly after or before new moon.
The phase in which exactly half of the visible disc of the Moon is bright.
The lit part of the Moon gets bigger from day to day.
A common name for the second full moon in a calendar month.

gewusst: A blue moon is not blue; the name just means that it is a rare event.
A lunar eclipse can only happen at full moon, a solar eclipse only at new moon.
Astronauts on the Moon also see the Earth in phases, just the exact opposite of our phases of the Moon.

teile.einleitung: Muscle output tells you how much work a person or animal can do with their muscles per second. Like the power of machines, it is measured in watts. A healthy person can manage about 100 watts over a longer time, as much as a bright old light bulb uses.
wichtigste: Power is work divided by time and is measured in watts.
A healthy person can produce about 100 watts over a longer time.
You only reach your highest power briefly, for example in a sprint.
Muscles have an efficiency of about 25 per cent.
Most of the energy turns into heat, which is why we get warm during sport.
In cycling, riders are compared using watts per kilogram.
A cyclist weighing 70 kg who produces 280 W manages 4 W/kg.

abschnitte.text: In physics, **power** is the work done in a certain time. If you lift something faster, the power is greater, even though the work stays the same. The unit is the **watt**, named after the Scot James Watt. One watt means one joule of work per second.

When you lift a mass, the work is weight times height. An example: 30 squats in 60 seconds, each lifting 40 kg by 0.4 m. With 10 N/kg, each squat gives 160 joules, 4800 joules altogether, and divided by 60 seconds that makes **80 watts**. If you lift a 2 kg dumbbell 0.5 m twenty times in 10 seconds, that is 20 watts.

How much power you can produce depends strongly on how long you keep it up. Over hours, a healthy person manages about **100 watts**, for example when cycling at an easy pace. Well-trained professional cyclists can hold several hundred watts for an hour. In a short **sprint** of a few seconds, top athletes even reach over 1000 watts.

Muscles turn only about a quarter of the energy from food into movement. This **efficiency** of around 25 per cent means that 400 watts of energy use produce about 100 watts of mechanical power. The remaining three quarters become heat. That is why we sweat during sport: the sweat cools the skin as it evaporates.

In cycling, especially uphill, it is not only power that counts but also body weight. That is why power is divided by mass, giving **watts per kilogram**. A cyclist weighing 70 kg who produces 280 watts reaches 4 W/kg. A light rider with the same W/kg is about as fast uphill as a heavy one.

In the past, power was measured in horsepower; one horsepower is around 735 watts. So over time a person produces much less than a horse. A small car, on the other hand, has a power of many thousands of watts. Even so, a person on a bicycle is one of the most efficient means of getting around there is.

begriffe.erklaerung: Work done per unit of time.
The unit of power, one joule per second.
The share of energy that is turned into useful work.
A training machine, for example an exercise bike, that measures power in watts.

gewusst: Anyone who cycles at 100 watts for an hour could in theory keep a light bulb glowing for an hour.
In very short sprints on the cycling track, the best sprinters reach peak power of well over 2000 watts.
A person at rest turns about as much energy into heat as a lamp of around 80 to 100 watts.

teile.einleitung: Moore's law is an observation from computer technology: the number of transistors on a computer chip doubles roughly every two years. It is not a law of nature but a rule of thumb that held true for a surprisingly long time. It is named after Gordon Moore, one of the founders of the company Intel.
wichtigste: Moore's law says that the number of transistors on chips doubles roughly every two years.
Gordon Moore described this development in a famous article in 1965.
It describes exponential growth.
In 10 years, the number of transistors therefore grows by a factor of 32.
Dennard scaling has no longer applied since the mid-2000s.
With very small transistors, quantum effects such as electron tunnelling cause problems.
With “More than Moore”, engineers look for new ways, such as stacked chips or specialised chips.

abschnitte.text: Gordon Moore lived from 1929 to 2023 and was an American chemist. In 1968, together with Robert Noyce, he founded the company **Intel**, which is now one of the largest chip makers in the world. In 1965 he wrote an article predicting how the number of components on chips would develop. At first he assumed it would double every year; in 1975 he corrected this to about two years.

A **transistor** is a tiny electrical switch made of semiconductor material, usually silicon. It can switch current on and off and so represent the zeros and ones of a computer. The more transistors a chip has, the more it can calculate and store at the same time. Modern transistors are so small that you can only see them with an electron microscope.

Doubling means that 1 becomes 2, then 4, 8, 16 and 32. After 10 years of doubling every two years, the number is therefore 32 times as large. This **exponential growth** quickly becomes enormous. The first microprocessor, the Intel 4004 from 1971, had around 2300 transistors; according to the rule there would have been around 2.4 billion in 2011, and that roughly matched real chips.

Thanks to this development, computers became ever faster, smaller and cheaper. A mobile phone today calculates much faster than the largest computers of the 1970s. As of 2026, the largest chips contain more than a hundred billion transistors. Without this progress there would be no smartphones, no fast internet and no artificial intelligence as we know it.

For a long time, smaller transistors did not increase the power use per area; this is called **Dennard scaling**. Since the mid-2000s, this rule no longer applies, because chips would get too hot. That is why the clock speed has hardly risen since then, and several processor cores are built in instead. With structures of only a few nanometres, **quantum effects** also cause problems: electrons tunnel through barrier layers that should actually stop them.

Experts are looking for new ways to make chips more powerful anyway. Chips are stacked on top of each other, specialised chips are built for particular tasks such as artificial intelligence, or many small chips are joined together in one package. This strategy is called **More than Moore**. Research is also going into completely new ideas such as quantum computers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny electrical switch, the basic building block of every computer chip.
Growth in which an amount keeps doubling at equal intervals of time.
A material such as silicon that conducts electricity or not, depending on the conditions.
The main processing chip of a computer.

gewusst: Moore's law is more of a self-fulfilling prophecy, because the chip industry used it as a target for decades.
Modern transistors are thousands of times thinner than a human hair.
The name “Moore's law” was not thought up by Gordon Moore himself; other people later called it that.

teile.einleitung: The Millikan experiment is a famous experiment in which the American physicist Robert Millikan determined the smallest electric charge around 1910. To do this, he watched tiny, electrically charged oil droplets between two metal plates. The result showed that electric charge only comes in fixed, smallest portions.
wichtigste: Around 1910, Robert Millikan measured the elementary charge very precisely.
He watched charged oil droplets in an electric field between two plates.
A floating droplet shows that the electric force and the weight are equal.
Oil was chosen because it hardly evaporates, so the mass of the droplets stays the same.
Millikan worked out the radius of the droplets using Stokes' law.
All the charges he measured were whole-number multiples of the elementary charge of about 1.6 · 10^-19 coulombs.
Millikan received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1923.

abschnitte.text: Robert Andrews Millikan lived from 1868 to 1953 and was a physicist from the USA. He did research at the University of Chicago and later at the California Institute of Technology. His student **Harvey Fletcher** helped him with his famous experiment. Millikan received the **Nobel Prize** in Physics in 1923 for measuring the elementary charge and for work on the photoelectric effect.

An atomiser sprays very fine oil droplets into a small chamber. Some droplets become electrically charged by friction. They pass between two horizontal metal plates, a **parallel-plate capacitor**, which has a voltage across it. Through a microscope you can watch the lit-up droplets, which look like little stars.

A droplet is pulled down by its weight and pushed up by the **electric force**. If you set the voltage exactly right, the droplet floats still in the air. Then the weight equals the electric force, so m · g = q · U / d. An example: a droplet of 4.9 · 10^-15 kg floats at 1500 volts with the plates 5 mm apart, so it carries about 1.6 · 10^-19 coulombs.

The droplets are so small that you cannot weigh them. So Millikan let them sink without any voltage and measured how fast they fell. Using **Stokes' law** about friction in air, he could work out their radius and therefore their mass. The buoyancy in air can often be ignored, because air has a much lower density than oil.

Millikan measured a great many droplets and kept finding similar values. All the charges were whole-number multiples of one smallest charge, the **elementary charge**. Today it is known very precisely: it is about 1.602 · 10^-19 coulombs. An electron carries exactly one such negative charge.

The experiment was important proof that electricity is made up of tiny particles. With the elementary charge, scientists could also calculate the mass of an electron. Since 2019, the value of the elementary charge has been fixed in the International System of Units. The Millikan experiment is still rebuilt at many upper secondary schools today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest electric charge found freely, about 1.6 · 10^-19 coulombs.
The unit of electric charge, named after Charles-Augustin de Coulomb.
Two parallel metal plates with an electric field between them.
A formula for the friction force on a small ball moving through air or a liquid.

gewusst: One coulomb is the charge of around six quintillion electrons.
Millikan watched some droplets for hours by steering them up and down again and again with the voltage.
The droplets in the experiment are so small that you can only see them as glowing dots in a microscope.
